# Using the Airtable MCP server

Last updated: November 9, 2026

Plan availability  | All plans
Permissions  | Your MCP permissions mirror the same permission level(s) that you have have been granted in Airtable.

  * Owner, Creator, or Editor - Can set up OAuth integrations and manage MCP access. Can read and update records they have permission to access.
    * Additionally, workspace owners or creators can create new bases via MCP. Note that base-level creator permissions will not be able to create a new base.
  * Commenter or Read-only - Can read data via MCP for bases they have access
Platform(s)  | Works with AI assistants that support Model Context Protocol (Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible tools)

Airtable’s MCP server lets you connect AI tools directly to your Airtable bases. This integration allows you to ask questions about your data, create and update records, and analyze information—all through natural conversation with AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and more.

Setup instructions, client quickstart guides, and full technical documentation are available at Airtable developer docs: MCP server overview.

pages.title: Creating personal access tokens (https://support.airtable.com/articles/9934989703-creating-personal-access-tokens)
pages.text: Creating personal access tokens | Airtable Help Center Contact support Sign up for free Creating personal access tokens Last updated 9 days ago Plan availability All plan types. Certain features are only available to Enterprise Scale or Business plan customers. Permissions The scopes and access that you can set up with personal access tokens will reflect the permissions that you have in the various workspaces and bases connected to your Airtable account. Platform(s) Web/Browser, Mac app, and Windows app Related reading Scopes developer documentation - More technical information related to scopes in Airtable. Service accounts overview - Help article that explains how Airtable admins can set up non-user accounts that can access Airtable's APIs. Third-party integrations via OAuth overview - Help article that discusses the broader ways to manage which third-party integrations have access to your Airtable data. What are personal access tokens? Personal access tokens (PATs) allow users to create multiple access tokens that allow for a wide range of access to the information held in Airtable bases. For example, on the narrow end, you can create a PAT that only has a single scope to a single base in Airtable. On the deep end, however, you could have a "main/overarching" token that has access to all workspaces and bases with all available scopes included. Further, admins can adopt user role access on workspaces and bases in their enterprise for which they are not direct collaborators. PATs allow admins access to workspaces and bases added to their organization. The admin who owns the PAT does not need to be a direct collaborator on every workspace and base within the organization. Instead, the PAT adopts the user role permissions for those bases and workspaces. Accessing personal access tokens Open the developer hub . Click Personal access tokens under the “Developers” section. Creating personal access tokens Open the developer hub . Click Create token . Name your token. Click + Add a scope . Check out developer documentation to learn more about scopes. Click + Add all resources / + Add a base to select your token’s access level. Options include choosing a single base, multiple bases—including bases from different workspaces—all current and future bases in a workspace you have access to, or even all of the bases in every workspace you have access to, including bases and workspaces added in the future. What the token can do in each base still depends on your permission level there. In the resource picker you can search for a base or workspace by its ID as well as by its name. This is useful when several bases share a similar name, or when you already have the base ID from a URL or an API response. Updating personal access tokens Open the developer hub . Scroll or search for the name of the PAT that you want to update/edit. Click the token's name. Alternatively, click the … icon to the far side of the PAT, then click Edit token . Update the name, scopes, or access for the PAT. Click Save changes . Regenerating or deleting personal access tokens Open the developer hub . Scroll or search for the name of the PAT that you want to regenerate or delete. Click the … icon to the far side of the PAT. Click Regenerate token or Delete token . Regenerating a token will cause a warning message to appear. Remember that any services currently using this token will need to be updated with the new token that is generated. Limiting a token to a specific set of bases You can't scope a personal access token to a managed app or to any other custom group of bases. Tokens can be scoped to individual bases, to workspaces, to all of your workspaces, or, for enterprise admins, to an entire organization. To give a token access to a specific set of bases—including bases added later—keep those bases in a dedicated workspace and add that workspace to the token. Create a workspace for the bases the token needs to reach. Move the bases into that workspace, or create them there. Add the account that will own the token to the workspace. For integrations, this is usually a service account. Open the developer hub while signed in as that account, and create a new token or open an existing one. Click + Add a base , then select the workspace. The token checks which workspace a base is in each time it's used. Bases created in or moved into the workspace later are covered automatically, and a base moved out of the workspace loses access right away. You don't need to own the workspace to add it to a token, but the token can only do what your permission level allows in each base—for example, Editor to update records and Creator to change fields and tables. If your organization's admin has turned on "Block API access to organization-owned bases and workspaces," the account must also be on the API access allowlist. FAQs What can my personal access tokens access? Unlike legacy API keys, which have the same access as your Airtable account, you can limit and configure the access of your personal access tokens. You can do this by selecting the scopes (what endpoints the token can use) and access/resources (which bases and workspaces the token can access) when creating or updating a token. Regardless of the scopes and access a user selects for their token, the token will only be able to perform actions that the user creating it is allowed to do. For example, to create a new field in a base via the API, the user must be a Creator collaborator in the base and the token must have the schema.bases:write scope and the base added as a resource. For more information about how scopes and access work, see the Authentication developer reference . For more information about configuring your token's access, refer to the personal access tokens guide . How do I find my API key? On Jan 18, 2023, we began the deprecating user API keys, completing the deprecation process on Feb 1, 2024, meaning: API Keys can no longer access the Airtable API. Webhooks created with user API keys will not expire, but can no longer be created. All users should migrate to personal access tokens for individual use and OAuth for third-party integrations. To access your PATs: Open the developer hub . Click Personal access tokens under the “Developers” section. Why might I be seeing the "INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND" error? Typically, this error type indicates either: A permissions-related issue, in which case you’ll want to: Check your PAT scopes Check your permissions level in the base you are referencing See if field and table permissions might also be causing the invalid permissions error. An issue with the base referenced, in which case you’ll want to: Double-check that the base id referenced is correct Confirm that the base has not been deleted More common API troubleshooting information is available here . I’m not able to access the enterprise scopes. What might be occurring? The ability to add enterprise. scopes is restricted to Enterprise Scale plans. This feature is not available on Business plans. Upgrading to an Enterprise Scale plan is required to use this functionality. Do personal access tokens expire? By default, no. A personal access token has no expiration window of its own and stays active until it is deleted, regenerated, or modified. One exception applies: on enterprise organizations, an admin can set a policy that caps the maximum lifetime of a personal access token. When a token passes that cap, requests using it fail with UNAUTHORIZED - Invalid authentication token . If you're on an enterprise organization and a token that previously worked stops being accepted, ask your admin whether a token lifetime policy is in effect. If no lifetime policy applies and a PAT stops working, the cause is one of the following rather than expiration: The token was regenerated, which invalidates the previous token value, so any service still using the old string will fail until updated with the new one. The token was deleted, or its scopes or base/workspace access were changed. If a PAT failure is happening in the environment or application consuming the token, check there, and with that platform's support, if Airtable shows the token as active. You can review your tokens any time in the developer hub under Personal access tokens. I have checked my scopes and IDs and still get an INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND error. What else could cause it? If your scopes, workspace/base IDs, and access all check out and you're on an enterprise organization, the most likely cause is an org-level API restriction set in the admin panel, not your token. When an admin enables "Block API access to organization-owned bases and workspaces" (under Settings → Integrations & development), only users on the API access allowlist can use personal access tokens against organization-owned resources — and requests from anyone not on the allowlist return INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND , even with fully correct scopes and IDs. To resolve it, ask one of your internal Airtable admins to add you (or your service account) to the allowlist for that setting. If the admin needs guidance, point them to Settings – Airtable admin panel. The other documented causes remain worth ruling out: field/table editing permissions and an incorrect or inaccessible base/workspace ID. Can I use a personal access token to write to a synced table? No. You can't create or delete records in a synced table, or edit its synced fields, with a personal access token, whatever scopes the token has. A synced table takes its values from its source, so Airtable returns an error such as Your record could not be created because the underlying table is externally synced. This also applies indirectly: a write to a linked record field fails if it would need to create a new record in a synced table. You can still write to fields you've added to the synced table yourself. Automations can't write to one-way synced tables; with two-way sync, automation actions (but not scripts) can make the edits the sync allows. Can I limit a personal access token to a single interface? No, you cannot scope a personal access token to an interface or to an individual view. Token access is granted per base and per workspace, so a token can reach any table or interface in a base it has access to, within the limits of its scopes. If your team works only in interfaces and you need to narrow what a token can reach in the underlying data, use Airtable field and table editing permissions on the tables and fields themselves. Those permissions are honored by API requests, just as they are in the Airtable UI. Why does my personal access token return "UNAUTHORIZED - Invalid authentication token"? This error means Airtable did not accept the credential sent in your request's Authorization header. It returns HTTP status 401 with this body: {"error":{"type":"UNAUTHORIZED","message":"Invalid authentication token"}} It is a different error from AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED , which means no credential reached Airtable at all, and from INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND , which means the token was accepted but doesn't have the scopes or resource access the request needs. A token that is rejected here never got as far as a scope or base check, so re-checking scopes and base access won't resolve it. Work through these causes in order: Only the token ID was sent. A complete token is a 17-character ID, a period, then a 64-character secret. The secret is displayed only once, at creation. If you no longer have it, regenerate the token and copy the whole value. The secret was truncated or altered between copying and sending. Check for missing characters, added whitespace, or a line break introduced by the tool storing the token. The token was deleted, regenerated, or had its access modified after you copied it. Confirm it still appears in the developer hub. The token has passed a maximum lifetime set by an admin. On enterprise organizations, an admin policy can cap how long a personal access token stays valid. Once a token is past that cap, every request using it returns this error even though the token still looks correct and still appears in your token list. Ask one of your Airtable admins whether a token lifetime policy applies to your organization. The endpoint doesn't accept personal access tokens. A small number of endpoints accept only other credential types, and a personal access token sent to one returns this error regardless of its scopes. To narrow down which of these applies, repeat the request with response headers shown — for example, curl -i instead of curl -s : If the response includes a WWW-Authenticate header containing error="invalid_token" , Airtable recognized the value as a personal access token and rejected it during validation. The cause is one of the token-specific items above. If that header is absent, the value wasn't recognized as a personal access token at all. Look for a malformed or truncated credential, or an endpoint that doesn't accept personal access tokens. For error codes beyond authentication, see Airtable API: Common troubleshooting . Never paste a complete token into a support ticket, community post, or chat conversation. Redact everything after the period, and regenerate any token whose secret you've shared. pages.text: Using the Airtable MCP server | Airtable Help Center Contact support Sign up for free Using the Airtable MCP server Last updated 13 days ago Plan availability All plans Permissions Your MCP permissions mirror the same permission level(s) that you have have been granted in Airtable. Owner , Creator , or Editor - Can set up OAuth integrations and manage MCP access. Can read and update records they have permission to access. Additionally, workspace owners or creators can create new bases via MCP. Note that base-level creator permissions will not be able to create a new base. Commenter or Read-only - Can read data via MCP for bases they have access Platform(s) Works with AI assistants that support Model Context Protocol (Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible tools) Airtable’s MCP server lets you connect AI tools directly to your Airtable bases. This integration allows you to ask questions about your data, create and update records, and analyze information—all through natural conversation with AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and more. Setup instructions, client quickstart guides, and full technical documentation are available at Airtable developer docs: MCP server overview . Start there to connect Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Cursor, or any other MCP-compatible tool. What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)? Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that allows AI tools to securely connect to external data sources. With MCP, AI tools can query your Airtable data, perform actions on your behalf, and present structured information—all while respecting your existing permissions and security settings. What you can do with MCP? The Airtable MCP Server enables several types of interactions between your AI tools and your data. Below is a brief list of capabilities, but you can find more information in the developer docs here . Search and analyze data - "Show me all customers from our CRM base who haven't been contacted in the last 30 days." Create records - "Add these 5 new project tasks to my 'Project Tracker' base." Update existing records - "Update the status of task #123 to 'Complete'." Create bases - "Create a new base called 'Q3 Campaign Tracker' in my Marketing workspace." Access interface data - "Show me the records from the 'Q1 Pipeline' page." (This works even with interface-only permissions, on supported page layouts) Create interfaces and interface pages - "Create an interface page to track my open tasks." Read and edit record detail pages - "Add the Owner and Due date fields to the record detail page on my 'Q1 Pipeline' page, and group them under 'Ownership'." Create and edit custom elements - "Build me a modern, sleek visual read out of the weekly data for our team's sprints from the 'Sprint' table." Build forms - "Create one form to intake feedback from an internal audience and another one from an external audience in the 'Product feedback' table." Submit forms on your behalf - "I found a bug in our software. I've attached screenshots and several logs of the issue, use that to file the request on my behalf to this form: {Insert a link to the Airtable form here}." Work with automations - “What automations are configured in my 'Project Tracker' base?” MCP prerequisites Before setting up the Airtable MCP Server, you'll need: An MCP-enabled Host (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, etc) Data stored in Airtable bases Permission to use third-party integrations in your Airtable organization (if you don’t have permission, an Airtable admin at your organization may need to allow-list a new integration) Tips for optimal MCP usage Get the most out of your MCP integration with these tips: Be specific : When asking about data, mention the base name or describe what you're looking for clearly Use natural language : You don't need to know field names or table IDs—describe what you want in plain English. Sometimes you may want to describe the base in more detail before asking for data from a table. Check permissions : If you can't access certain data via MCP, verify that you have the appropriate permissions in Airtable. Think about what data you’re giving your AI tool : Your tool will be able to read and make edits to your Airtable data on your behalf. Make sure you trust the tools you’re using or any other data sources you connect to. Setting up a quick MCP connection All setup paths—pre-built connectors, plugins, manual OAuth configuration, and personal access tokens—are documented in the developer docs: MCP server overview and setup Claude quickstart steps Claude Code quickstart steps ChatGPT quickstart steps Before setting up, you'll need an MCP-enabled AI tool, data stored in Airtable bases, and permission to use third-party integrations in your Airtable organization. If you don't have permission, an Airtable admin may need to allowlist the integration— see the FAQs below . Managing your MCP integration After setup, you can control which bases your AI assistant can access: Go to your third-party integrations page . Alternatively, click your user profile in Airtable, then click Integrations and Third-party integrations . Select your MCP integration. Add or remove bases and apps as needed. You can also add apps where you have interface-only access. Limitations and dependencies Keep these limitations in mind while using the MCP Server: Rate limits : MCP server calls are subject to standard Airtable API rate limits . Batch size : Creating records is limited to 10 records per request. Change policy : Tool names, behaviors, and capabilities may change Permission requirements : The MCP server respects your existing Airtable permissions—you can only access data you normally have permission to view or modify. Third-party integrations : If you are an enterprise user and your admin has enabled restrictions on third-party integrations, they'll need to allowlist the MCP integration. Automation activation : MCP can create and update automation drafts, but turning an automation on (deploy) is done in the Airtable UI. Automations with Script actions : MCP can create and update automation drafts, but automations containing a Script action can't be created or edited via MCP. You will need to add or modify Script actions directly in the Airtable UI. Interface filters : MCP can't add filters to an Interface (for example, a Current User filter). You will need to configure Interface filters directly in Interface Designer. Editing existing Interfaces : Some page types, including inbox and legacy layouts, can only be edited in Interface Designer by a user, manually. MCP can edit pages in an existing Interface directly. It can change settings on grid, list, kanban, calendar, gallery and timeline pages, and it can edit dashboards, standalone forms and record detail pages. On record detail pages it can add or remove fields, add groups, change the title field and how fields are displayed, and make the page read-only. To make bigger structural changes to an interface page, such as changing its type, replace its layout through MCP or use Interface Designer. Interface page layouts : The page-read tools support most, but not all, interface page layouts. If a page's layout isn't supported yet, the request fails, and your AI assistant may report that no matching records were found rather than that the page type isn't supported. Ask for a record list or grid page sourced from the same data, or ask a base Owner or Creator to grant you read-only base access so your assistant can use the table and view tools instead. Troubleshooting MCP connection problems If your AI tool can't connect to the Airtable MCP server, work through the checks below before contacting support. Your client reports "authentication required" and lists no tools Your client reached the server but hasn't finished the OAuth login. Run your client's MCP login command and complete the Airtable authorization in your browser. If the authorization page returns an error instead, see the next section. Authorization fails with " invalid client_id or mismatched redirect_uri " The full error reads: " This third-party app failed to properly construct a request to Airtable: invalid client_id or mismatched redirect_uri ." Some MCP clients register themselves with Airtable using Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) rather than dynamic client registration, and that path can be rejected at authorization. Airtable's OAuth metadata advertises a dynamic client registration endpoint, so telling your client to use dynamic client registration resolves the error. In Codex CLI, force dynamic client registration when you log in: codex mcp login airtable --oauth-client-registration dcr In other clients, look for an equivalent OAuth setting that selects dynamic client registration — sometimes labeled DCR — as the registration method. If your client doesn't expose that option, connect with a personal access token instead; see the MCP server overview in the developer docs. This workaround was reported against Codex CLI 0.166.0 on macOS. Other clients and operating systems may name the setting differently. Your client isn't one of the documented quickstarts The developer docs carry step-by-step quickstarts for a few clients, but any tool that supports remote MCP servers over HTTP can connect. Point it at the server URL https://mcp.airtable.com/mcp and choose OAuth as the authentication method, then follow the error guidance above if authorization fails. Your admin hasn't allowlisted the integration If your organization restricts third-party integrations, the MCP integration must be allowlisted before you can connect. See "How can admins enable a blocked MCP integration?" in the FAQs below. If the connection still fails after these steps, see Troubleshooting disconnected OAuth integrations in Airtable . FAQs Can I use MCP with any base I have access to? If you have base-level access, you can use MCP to access the data stored within that base. The MCP server respects your existing Airtable permissions. If you have read-only or comment-only access to a base, you'll be able to read that data via MCP, but you won't be able to create or update records. What AI assistants work with Airtable's MCP Server? Any AI assistant that supports the Model Context Protocol can connect to Airtable's MCP Server. This includes Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible tools. Check your AI assistant's documentation to confirm MCP support. How do I revoke access if I no longer want my AI assistant to access my bases? Navigate to your user profile > Integrations > Third-party Integrations, find the MCP integration, and either remove specific bases or delete the integration entirely. Does using MCP count against my Airtable limits? MCP uses our public API under the hood and will count against any existing API rate limits. Any records created using MCP will count against existing base limits. Can I use MCP to access Airtable Interfaces? Yes, for supported page layouts. If you have interface-only access to a base, you can use MCP to discover your interface pages ( list_pages_for_base ), list records shown on a page ( list_records_for_page ), and drill into record details ( get_record_for_page ). The data returned respects the same permissions as your interface—you'll only see data that your interface pages make available to you. Not every interface page layout is supported yet. If a page's layout isn't supported, the request fails and your assistant may say that no matching records were found. See " Limitations and dependencies " above. What happens if I try to update a field I don't have permission to modify? The MCP server will return an error, just as the Airtable API would. Your AI assistant should communicate this limitation to you. Are there additional costs for using MCP? No. The MCP integration is currently included with your current Airtable plan. There are no additional Airtable charges for MCP usage, but existing API rate limits remain. How can admins enable a blocked MCP integration? For Airtable admins to enable a blocked integration: Navigate to Admin Panel > Settings > Integrations & development > Third party integration allowlist. Click Allow integration . Enter the client ID provided by your user. Click Save . Can I create new bases using MCP? Yes. You can use the create_base tool to create a new base in any workspace where you have Creator-level permissions. You can optionally define tables and fields during creation. Use list_workspaces first to find the workspace ID where you want to create the base. Can the Airtable MCP connect to development apps (part of the managed apps and components feature ) and update those apps in the same way as regular Airtable bases? No. Calls to a development base will return a 403 permissions error. However, API/MCP calls can be made to bases where a managed app or component has been installed (i.e., the child/production bases). So the restriction is specifically on the development base itself, not on installed instances. How do I connect Claude Code to Airtable? The recommended approach is to run claude mcp add --transport http airtable https://mcp.airtable.com/mcp in your terminal, then run /mcp inside Claude Code to authenticate with your Airtable account through your browser. Alternatively, you can connect using a personal access token if you prefer. See Airtable developer docs: MCP server overview for instructions. Who at my organization can enable third-party integrations or MCP, and can Airtable tell me who my admin is? Allowlisting a third-party integration is handled by an admin at your own organization. Typically that person is a super admin, org unit admin, or an integration admin with access to the “Settings → Integrations & development” in the admin panel. For the exact steps, see "How can admins enable a blocked MCP integration?" above. For privacy and security reasons, Airtable Support does not share the names or contact details of admins within an enterprise account. To find the right person, reach out to your internal IT team or whoever manages your organization's Airtable account. If your first contact isn't able to make an organization-wide decision, they can usually point you to the person who can. I have Editor permissions but can only create an "Interface only" token. Why? If you are only able to create "Interface only" tokens, that usually means you have Editor access to an interface, not to the underlying base. Interface access and base access are separate in Airtable, and full-access tokens — including the kind needed to connect an MCP client like Claude in edit mode — require base-level access. To resolve it, ask a base owner, creator, or an admin in your organization to grant you Editor (or higher) access to the base itself, not just the interface. Base access is shared through a base invite link, which works differently from interface sharing — see Creating Airtable base share links. Once you have base-level access, the full-access token option will become available. How do I limit write access when setting up an MCP connection? For a read-only connection, so your AI tool can view data but can't create, update, or delete records, include only these scopes: data.records:read schema.bases:read data.recordComments:read workspacesAndBases:read Enterprise admins can use a service account for this setup. See Airtable developer docs: MCP server overview . Can I create or edit automations using MCP? Yes. You can list and inspect automations, create draft automations, update draft configuration, and delete inactive automations. New and updated automations are saved as drafts—open the automation in Airtable to review and turn it on. To delete an automation that is currently on, turn it off in Airtable first. pages.title: Creating personal access tokens (https://support.airtable.com/articles/9934989703-Creating-personal-access-tokens)
pages.text: Creating personal access tokens | Airtable Help Center Contact support Sign up for free Creating personal access tokens Last updated 9 days ago Plan availability All plan types. Certain features are only available to Enterprise Scale or Business plan customers. Permissions The scopes and access that you can set up with personal access tokens will reflect the permissions that you have in the various workspaces and bases connected to your Airtable account. Platform(s) Web/Browser, Mac app, and Windows app Related reading Scopes developer documentation - More technical information related to scopes in Airtable. Service accounts overview - Help article that explains how Airtable admins can set up non-user accounts that can access Airtable's APIs. Third-party integrations via OAuth overview - Help article that discusses the broader ways to manage which third-party integrations have access to your Airtable data. What are personal access tokens? Personal access tokens (PATs) allow users to create multiple access tokens that allow for a wide range of access to the information held in Airtable bases. For example, on the narrow end, you can create a PAT that only has a single scope to a single base in Airtable. On the deep end, however, you could have a "main/overarching" token that has access to all workspaces and bases with all available scopes included. Further, admins can adopt user role access on workspaces and bases in their enterprise for which they are not direct collaborators. PATs allow admins access to workspaces and bases added to their organization. The admin who owns the PAT does not need to be a direct collaborator on every workspace and base within the organization. Instead, the PAT adopts the user role permissions for those bases and workspaces. Accessing personal access tokens Open the developer hub . Click Personal access tokens under the “Developers” section. Creating personal access tokens Open the developer hub . Click Create token . Name your token. Click + Add a scope . Check out developer documentation to learn more about scopes. Click + Add all resources / + Add a base to select your token’s access level. Options include choosing a single base, multiple bases—including bases from different workspaces—all current and future bases in a workspace you have access to, or even all of the bases in every workspace you have access to, including bases and workspaces added in the future. What the token can do in each base still depends on your permission level there. In the resource picker you can search for a base or workspace by its ID as well as by its name. This is useful when several bases share a similar name, or when you already have the base ID from a URL or an API response. Updating personal access tokens Open the developer hub . Scroll or search for the name of the PAT that you want to update/edit. Click the token's name. Alternatively, click the … icon to the far side of the PAT, then click Edit token . Update the name, scopes, or access for the PAT. Click Save changes . Regenerating or deleting personal access tokens Open the developer hub . Scroll or search for the name of the PAT that you want to regenerate or delete. Click the … icon to the far side of the PAT. Click Regenerate token or Delete token . Regenerating a token will cause a warning message to appear. Remember that any services currently using this token will need to be updated with the new token that is generated. Limiting a token to a specific set of bases You can't scope a personal access token to a managed app or to any other custom group of bases. Tokens can be scoped to individual bases, to workspaces, to all of your workspaces, or, for enterprise admins, to an entire organization. To give a token access to a specific set of bases—including bases added later—keep those bases in a dedicated workspace and add that workspace to the token. Create a workspace for the bases the token needs to reach. Move the bases into that workspace, or create them there. Add the account that will own the token to the workspace. For integrations, this is usually a service account. Open the developer hub while signed in as that account, and create a new token or open an existing one. Click + Add a base , then select the workspace. The token checks which workspace a base is in each time it's used. Bases created in or moved into the workspace later are covered automatically, and a base moved out of the workspace loses access right away. You don't need to own the workspace to add it to a token, but the token can only do what your permission level allows in each base—for example, Editor to update records and Creator to change fields and tables. If your organization's admin has turned on "Block API access to organization-owned bases and workspaces," the account must also be on the API access allowlist. FAQs What can my personal access tokens access? Unlike legacy API keys, which have the same access as your Airtable account, you can limit and configure the access of your personal access tokens. You can do this by selecting the scopes (what endpoints the token can use) and access/resources (which bases and workspaces the token can access) when creating or updating a token. Regardless of the scopes and access a user selects for their token, the token will only be able to perform actions that the user creating it is allowed to do. For example, to create a new field in a base via the API, the user must be a Creator collaborator in the base and the token must have the schema.bases:write scope and the base added as a resource. For more information about how scopes and access work, see the Authentication developer reference . For more information about configuring your token's access, refer to the personal access tokens guide . How do I find my API key? On Jan 18, 2023, we began the deprecating user API keys, completing the deprecation process on Feb 1, 2024, meaning: API Keys can no longer access the Airtable API. Webhooks created with user API keys will not expire, but can no longer be created. All users should migrate to personal access tokens for individual use and OAuth for third-party integrations. To access your PATs: Open the developer hub . Click Personal access tokens under the “Developers” section. Why might I be seeing the "INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND" error? Typically, this error type indicates either: A permissions-related issue, in which case you’ll want to: Check your PAT scopes Check your permissions level in the base you are referencing See if field and table permissions might also be causing the invalid permissions error. An issue with the base referenced, in which case you’ll want to: Double-check that the base id referenced is correct Confirm that the base has not been deleted More common API troubleshooting information is available here . I’m not able to access the enterprise scopes. What might be occurring? The ability to add enterprise. scopes is restricted to Enterprise Scale plans. This feature is not available on Business plans. Upgrading to an Enterprise Scale plan is required to use this functionality. Do personal access tokens expire? By default, no. A personal access token has no expiration window of its own and stays active until it is deleted, regenerated, or modified. One exception applies: on enterprise organizations, an admin can set a policy that caps the maximum lifetime of a personal access token. When a token passes that cap, requests using it fail with UNAUTHORIZED - Invalid authentication token . If you're on an enterprise organization and a token that previously worked stops being accepted, ask your admin whether a token lifetime policy is in effect. If no lifetime policy applies and a PAT stops working, the cause is one of the following rather than expiration: The token was regenerated, which invalidates the previous token value, so any service still using the old string will fail until updated with the new one. The token was deleted, or its scopes or base/workspace access were changed. If a PAT failure is happening in the environment or application consuming the token, check there, and with that platform's support, if Airtable shows the token as active. You can review your tokens any time in the developer hub under Personal access tokens. I have checked my scopes and IDs and still get an INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND error. What else could cause it? If your scopes, workspace/base IDs, and access all check out and you're on an enterprise organization, the most likely cause is an org-level API restriction set in the admin panel, not your token. When an admin enables "Block API access to organization-owned bases and workspaces" (under Settings → Integrations & development), only users on the API access allowlist can use personal access tokens against organization-owned resources — and requests from anyone not on the allowlist return INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND , even with fully correct scopes and IDs. To resolve it, ask one of your internal Airtable admins to add you (or your service account) to the allowlist for that setting. If the admin needs guidance, point them to Settings – Airtable admin panel. The other documented causes remain worth ruling out: field/table editing permissions and an incorrect or inaccessible base/workspace ID. Can I use a personal access token to write to a synced table? No. You can't create or delete records in a synced table, or edit its synced fields, with a personal access token, whatever scopes the token has. A synced table takes its values from its source, so Airtable returns an error such as Your record could not be created because the underlying table is externally synced. This also applies indirectly: a write to a linked record field fails if it would need to create a new record in a synced table. You can still write to fields you've added to the synced table yourself. Automations can't write to one-way synced tables; with two-way sync, automation actions (but not scripts) can make the edits the sync allows. Can I limit a personal access token to a single interface? No, you cannot scope a personal access token to an interface or to an individual view. Token access is granted per base and per workspace, so a token can reach any table or interface in a base it has access to, within the limits of its scopes. If your team works only in interfaces and you need to narrow what a token can reach in the underlying data, use Airtable field and table editing permissions on the tables and fields themselves. Those permissions are honored by API requests, just as they are in the Airtable UI. Why does my personal access token return "UNAUTHORIZED - Invalid authentication token"? This error means Airtable did not accept the credential sent in your request's Authorization header. It returns HTTP status 401 with this body: {"error":{"type":"UNAUTHORIZED","message":"Invalid authentication token"}} It is a different error from AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED , which means no credential reached Airtable at all, and from INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND , which means the token was accepted but doesn't have the scopes or resource access the request needs. A token that is rejected here never got as far as a scope or base check, so re-checking scopes and base access won't resolve it. Work through these causes in order: Only the token ID was sent. A complete token is a 17-character ID, a period, then a 64-character secret. The secret is displayed only once, at creation. If you no longer have it, regenerate the token and copy the whole value. The secret was truncated or altered between copying and sending. Check for missing characters, added whitespace, or a line break introduced by the tool storing the token. The token was deleted, regenerated, or had its access modified after you copied it. Confirm it still appears in the developer hub. The token has passed a maximum lifetime set by an admin. On enterprise organizations, an admin policy can cap how long a personal access token stays valid. Once a token is past that cap, every request using it returns this error even though the token still looks correct and still appears in your token list. Ask one of your Airtable admins whether a token lifetime policy applies to your organization. The endpoint doesn't accept personal access tokens. A small number of endpoints accept only other credential types, and a personal access token sent to one returns this error regardless of its scopes. To narrow down which of these applies, repeat the request with response headers shown — for example, curl -i instead of curl -s : If the response includes a WWW-Authenticate header containing error="invalid_token" , Airtable recognized the value as a personal access token and rejected it during validation. The cause is one of the token-specific items above. If that header is absent, the value wasn't recognized as a personal access token at all. Look for a malformed or truncated credential, or an endpoint that doesn't accept personal access tokens. For error codes beyond authentication, see Airtable API: Common troubleshooting . Never paste a complete token into a support ticket, community post, or chat conversation. Redact everything after the period, and regenerate any token whose secret you've shared. Related Articles Getting started with Airtable's Web API Airtable Web API - Using filterByFormula or sort parameters Service accounts overview Airtable API: Common troubleshooting Managing API call limits in Airtable

The MCP server respects your existing Airtable permissions. If you have read-only or comment-only access to a base, you'll be able to read that data via MCP, but you won't be able to create or update records. What AI assistants work with Airtable's MCP Server? Any AI assistant that supports the Model Context Protocol can connect to Airtable's MCP Server. This includes Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible tools. Check your AI assistant's documentation to confirm MCP support. How do I revoke access if I no longer want my AI assistant to access my bases? Navigate to your user profile > Integrations > Third-party Integrations, find the MCP integration, and either remove specific bases or delete the integration entirely. Does using MCP count against my Airtable limits? MCP uses our public API under the hood and will count against any existing API rate limits. Any records created using MCP will count against existing base limits. Can I use MCP to access Airtable Interfaces? Yes, for supported page layouts. If you have interface-only access to a base, you can use MCP to discover your interface pages ( list_pages_for_base ), list records shown on a page ( list_records_for_page ), and drill into record details ( get_record_for_page ). The data returned respects the same permissions as your interface—you'll only see data that your interface pages make available to you. Not every interface page layout is supported yet. If a page's layout isn't supported, the request fails and your assistant may say that no matching records were found. See " Limitations and dependencies " above. What happens if I try to update a field I don't have permission to modify? The MCP server will return an error, just as the Airtable API would. Your AI assistant should communicate this limitation to you. Are there additional costs for using MCP? No. The MCP integration is currently included with your current Airtable plan. There are no additional Airtable charges for MCP usage, but existing API rate limits remain. How can admins enable a blocked MCP integration? For Airtable admins to enable a blocked integration: Navigate to Admin Panel > Settings > Integrations & development > Third party integration allowlist. Click Allow integration . Enter the client ID provided by your user. Click Save . Can I create new bases using MCP? Yes. You can use the create_base tool to create a new base in any workspace where you have Creator-level permissions. You can optionally define tables and fields during creation. Use list_workspaces first to find the workspace ID where you want to create the base. Can the Airtable MCP connect to development apps (part of the managed apps and components feature ) and update those apps in the same way as regular Airtable bases? No. Calls to a development base will return a 403 permissions error. However, API/MCP calls can be made to bases where a managed app or component has been installed (i.e., the child/production bases). So the restriction is specifically on the development base itself, not on installed instances. How do I connect Claude Code to Airtable? The recommended approach is to run claude mcp add --transport http airtable https://mcp.airtable.com/mcp in your terminal, then run /mcp inside Claude Code to authenticate with your Airtable account through your browser. Alternatively, you can connect using a personal access token if you prefer. See Airtable developer docs: MCP server overview for instructions. Who at my organization can enable third-party integrations or MCP, and can Airtable tell me who my admin is? Allowlisting a third-party integration is handled by an admin at your own organization. Typically that person is a super admin, org unit admin, or an integration admin with access to the “Settings → Integrations & development” in the admin panel. For the exact steps, see "How can admins enable a blocked MCP integration?" above. For privacy and security reasons, Airtable Support does not share the names or contact details of admins within an enterprise account. To find the right person, reach out to your internal IT team or whoever manages your organization's Airtable account. If your first contact isn't able to make an organization-wide decision, they can usually point you to the person who can. I have Editor permissions but can only create an "Interface only" token. Why? If you are only able to create "Interface only" tokens, that usually means you have Editor access to an interface, not to the underlying base. Interface access and base access are separate in Airtable, and full-access tokens — including the kind needed to connect an MCP client like Claude in edit mode — require base-level access. To resolve it, ask a base owner, creator, or an admin in your organization to grant you Editor (or higher) access to the base itself, not just the interface. Base access is shared through a base invite link, which works differently from interface sharing — see Creating Airtable base share links. Once you have base-level access, the full-access token option will become available. How do I limit write access when setting up an MCP connection? For a read-only connection, so your AI tool can view data but can't create, update, or delete records, include only these scopes: data.records:read schema.bases:read data.recordComments:read workspacesAndBases:read Enterprise admins can use a service account for this setup. See Airtable developer docs: MCP server overview . Can I create or edit automations using MCP? Yes. You can list and inspect automations, create draft automations, update draft configuration, and delete inactive automations. New and updated automations are saved as drafts—open the automation in Airtable to review and turn it on. To delete an automation that is currently on, turn it off in Airtable first. pages.text: AI agent software: Don’t just ask AI. Deploy it. | Airtable Airtable MCP Any agent. All your business context. One place to work. Connect Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and 3rd party model to Airtable. Work with live data, build apps, and create workflows in the same system your team uses. Connect your AI tool Book a demo Capabilities Ask about the data.  Or create the system that runs it Your agent connects to every part of Airtable: records, structure, interfaces, automations. Find out what's blocked this week, or have it stand up the tables and workflows behind the work, inside the base your team already works in. Work with your data Find the right bases, tables, and records. Ask about status, dependencies, and gaps. Then write the answer back into the base. Build your app Create bases, tables, and fields. Build interface pages and record views. Triage feedback into fixes Pull feedback from Airtable into your coding agent, ship the fix, and mark the record resolved. Governance Works within your permissions If you can't edit a base, neither can your agent. Anything it builds starts paused until you say go. Uses Airtable permissions A connected assistant can only perform actions allowed by your Airtable access and the authorization you grant. Review before workflows run Automations created through MCP arrive paused. You approve them and switch them on in Airtable. Managed centrally Organization admins can block MCP access using the available admin controls. Ways to start building Build Interfaces and Automations with MCP Let's Build Live: Airtable MCP Airtable MCP for teams: Submit forms, ask questions, and make updates – no base access needed You have questions? We have answers What is Airtable's MCP server? A hosted service at mcp.airtable.com/mcp that lets any MCP-compatible AI client read and act on live Airtable data and structure. Your agent can query records, build tables and fields, create and publish interfaces, and write automations. How much does it cost? Nothing. Today, MCP is available on every plan, including the free plan, at no additional cost. Which AI clients work with it? It works with any AI via MCP servers, with out of the box connections for Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini. Do I need an API token? No. Major clients connect over OAuth with a single sign-in. Nothing to generate, paste, or rotate. You can also create granular Personal Access Tokens to further scope access. What permissions does an agent get? Exactly the permissions of the person who connected it, and nothing more. MCP is not a separate access model. If you cannot edit a base, neither can your agent. Can an agent build things, or only read data? It can build. Agents create bases, tables, and fields, build and publish interface pages and forms, and write automations, alongside reading and updating records. What happens when an agent creates an automation? It arrives paused. A person reviews it in Airtable and activates it before it ever runs. Can admins turn MCP off? Yes. Admins can block MCP access across the organization or an org unit, the same way they block API access. What are the rate limits? MCP runs through the same public REST API, so the standard limits apply: 5 requests per second per base and 50 requests per second per token. Records an agent creates count against your base's normal record limits.
